title: Harnessing finite-size effects to gauge aging in the $2D$ Ising model
authors: Dustin Warkotsch, Malte Henkel, Wolfhard Janke
abstract: The relaxation behavior towards equilibrium of the $2D$ Ising model with nearest-neighbor interactions has been studied with focus on the two-time autocorrelator $C(t,s)$. Finite-size effects affecting the growing magnetic domains lead to the saturation of $C(t,s)$ with a distinct plateau of height $C_{\infty}^{(2)}(s,L)$ scaling algebraically with waiting time $s$ and lattice size $L$. These scaling relations are used to produce precise estimates for the autocorrelation exponent $λ$ and dynamical exponent $z$ with deliberately small lattices. Treating smooth domain walls in a similar manner to the lattice boundaries, their effect on $C(t,s)$ can be understood as premature finite-size phenomenon, extending our ansatz to systems not yet in equilibrium.
summary: This paper develops a novel computational method to determine critical exponents ($\lambda$ and $z$) in the aging dynamics of the 2D Ising model. It achieves this by deliberately exploiting finite-size effects observed in the two-time autocorrelator plateau height, providing robust estimates even when direct asymptotic analysis is difficult.
main_problem: The study aims to precisely gauge aging phenomena in systems far from equilibrium by analyzing the relaxation behavior of the 2D Ising model.
main_result: Finite-size scaling relations derived from the plateau height of the two-time autocorrelator allow for independent estimation of the autocorrelation exponent ($\lambda$) and dynamical exponent ($z$).
method: Classical Monte Carlo simulations are employed, utilizing finite-size scaling techniques to analyze how system size ($L$) affects the decay of the two-time autocorrelator $C(t,s)$.
model_or_system: The physical model is the 2D Ising model with nearest-neighbor interactions. The analysis focuses on its non-equilibrium dynamics following a quench below the critical temperature.
key_observables: Two-time autocorrelator $C(t, s)$, characteristic length scale $\ell(t)$, and the plateau height $C_{\infty}^{(2)}(s,L)$.
important_parameters: Temperature regime ($0 < T < T_c$), lattice size ($L$), waiting time ($s$), and the exponents $\lambda$ and $z$.
main_assumptions: The analysis treats domain wall effects as a 'premature finite-size phenomenon' and relies on specific scaling laws derived from the autocorrelator plateau.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crossover of both the length scale $\ell(t)$ and the autocorrelation $C(y, s)$ towards saturation plateaus when varying lattice sizes ($L$).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework using the two-time autocorrelator in finite systems. It then details the application of novel scaling relations to extract exponents ($\lambda$ and $\lambda/z$) by analyzing how these observables depend on $L$ and $s$.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the techniques for characterizing slow relaxation dynamics (aging) using finite-size effects are highly relevant to open quantum systems where thermalization or quasi-equilibrium states are approached slowly.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Exemplary behavior of the characteristic length scale ℓ(t) vs time t (upper curves, right and upper axes) and the two-time autocorrelator C(ys, s) vs y (lower curves, left and lower axes) for a nearest-neighbor 2D Ising model after a quench to 0.2Tc for system sizes L = {384, 448, 512, 640, 768} and waiting time s = 64. Note that saturation of both exhibits a step-wise behavior featuring the formation of an initial pseudo-plateau before settling at the equilibrium value beginning around t ≈1010 and y ≈108, respectively.

Figure 2. Heatmap of plateau heights C(2) ∞of the two-time autocorrelator at T = 0.2TC depending on linear lattice size L and waiting time s. As the plateau height grows from the lower left to the upper right side, equations (6) and (7) describe the relation between individual values of C(2) ∞for their respective orthogonal axis.

Figure 3. Two-time autocorrelator C(ys, s) for the 2D Ising model quenched to T = 0.2Tc for various fixed (a) lattice sizes L at s = 256, or (b) waiting times s at L = 768. The steps in the plateaus result from gradual evaporation of metastable, i.e., striped states of all kinds (viz. figure 4). The dashed black lines indicate the height C(2) ∞for the respective L or s.

Figure 4. Metastable states of the 2D Ising model with periodic boundary conditions: horizontal stripe, vertical stripe and diagonal stripe. The former two are infinitely long-lived at T = 0 whereas the lifetime of the last one depends on lattice size L. Above T = 0, all stripes evaporate eventually, at sufficiently large times.
Figure 5. Average lifetime (measured in MC sweeps) of all striped configurations vs lattice size L at T = 0.2Tc in 2D.
